course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

topic.title: Failure of Compromise
topic.summary: Why the Kansas–Nebraska Act, violence in Kansas, the Dred Scott decision, the Lincoln–Douglas debates, and John Brown's raid failed to settle the question of slavery and ended the old party system.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854 provided that
choices: slavery would be banned in the new territories north of 36°30′
Kansas would enter as a slave state and Nebraska would enter as a free state
settlers in Kansas and Nebraska would decide the question of slavery
the Missouri Compromise line would be extended west to the Pacific Ocean
questions.explanation: Douglas applied popular sovereignty to Kansas and Nebraska, and the Act repealed the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery north of the line.
choiceExplanations: The Act repealed that ban.
The Act did not set the status of either state.
Douglas applied popular sovereignty to Kansas and Nebraska, and the Act repealed the Missouri Compromise ban on slavery north of the line.
The Act repealed the line.
questions.distinguisher: The banned choice is close because Kansas and Nebraska lay north of the old line where slavery had been banned, but the Act repealed that ban.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect of the Kansas–Nebraska Act?
choices: It helped to bring about the Republican Party in the North
It settled the question of slavery in the territories for a generation
It united Northern and Southern Whigs behind the leadership of Douglas
It led the Southern Democrats to leave their party and form a new one
questions.explanation: Northern anger at the repeal of the Missouri Compromise brought together Free-Soilers, antislavery Whigs, and antislavery Democrats.
choiceExplanations: Northern anger at the repeal of the Missouri Compromise brought together Free-Soilers, antislavery Whigs, and antislavery Democrats.
Conflict increased after the Act.
The Whig Party broke apart.
That split came later, in 1860.
questions.distinguisher: The settled for a generation choice is close because Douglas hoped popular sovereignty would end the dispute, but the Act renewed it.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The Republican Party, formed in 1854, was united mainly by its opposition to
choices: slavery in every state of the Union, which its platform demanded be ended at once
the spread of slavery into the western territories
the political power of Catholic immigrants, which its leaders wanted to limit
the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the lands that it had added to the nation
questions.explanation: Republicans came together to keep slavery out of the territories, not to abolish it in the states.
choiceExplanations: The party did not demand an end to slavery in the states.
Republicans came together to keep slavery out of the territories, not to abolish it in the states.
That was the aim of the Know-Nothings.
The party did not oppose the treaty.
questions.distinguisher: The slavery in every state choice is close because Republicans disliked slavery, but their platform aimed at stopping its spread.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The violence in Kansas in 1856 is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A war between the United States and the Native nations of the Great Plains
A revolt by farmers against the tax on the railroad that crossed the territory
A boundary dispute between Missouri and Kansas over the course of a river
Rival efforts by proslavery and antislavery settlers to control the new territory
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty invited both sides to send settlers, and the contest for control turned violent.
choiceExplanations: The violence was between settlers.
No tax revolt took place.
The dispute concerned slavery and not a river.
Popular sovereignty invited both sides to send settlers, and the contest for control turned violent.
questions.distinguisher: The war with Native nations choice is close because Kansas was Native land before settlement, but the 1856 violence was between rival settlers.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), the Supreme Court ruled that
choices: Dred Scott was free because he had lived for years in a free territory
popular sovereignty was the only lawful way to decide the status of slavery
Congress had no power to ban slavery in the territories
free African Americans could be citizens of a state but not of the nation
questions.explanation: Chief Justice Taney wrote that Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories and that African Americans could not be citizens.
choiceExplanations: The Court ruled against him.
The Court did not endorse popular sovereignty.
Chief Justice Taney wrote that Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories and that African Americans could not be citizens.
The Court held that no African American could be a citizen.
questions.distinguisher: The freedom choice is close because Scott had sued on that ground, but the Court ruled that he remained enslaved.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect of the Dred Scott decision?
choices: It persuaded most Northerners to accept the spread of slavery into the territories
It ended the dispute over slavery in the territories for several years
It led Congress to repeal the Fugitive Slave Act in the same year
It angered many Northerners and strengthened the Republican Party
questions.explanation: The ruling denied the Republican goal of banning slavery in the territories and convinced many Northerners that a “slave power” controlled the government.
choiceExplanations: Most Northerners were angered.
The dispute increased.
The Act stayed in force until 1864.
The ruling denied the Republican goal of banning slavery in the territories and convinced many Northerners that a “slave power” controlled the government.
questions.distinguisher: The accept the spread choice is close because the Court's authority was great, but Northern voters rejected the ruling and turned to the Republicans.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between the Whig Party and the Republican Party?
choices: The Whigs opposed the spread of slavery, while the Republicans did not address it
The Whigs had Northern and Southern members, while the Republicans were a Northern party
The Whigs grew stronger in the 1850s, while the Republicans quickly declined
The Whigs were a sectional party of the South, while the Republicans were national
questions.explanation: The Whigs split over slavery, while the Republicans formed in the North and won no Southern electoral votes in 1860.
choiceExplanations: The Republicans were founded to oppose the spread of slavery.
The Whigs split over slavery, while the Republicans formed in the North and won no Southern electoral votes in 1860.
The Whigs collapsed and the Republicans grew.
The Whigs were national and the Republicans were Northern.
questions.distinguisher: The opposed the spread choice is close because some Whigs were antislavery, but the party as a whole did not take that position.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Why did Douglas's answer at Freeport in 1858 anger many Southern Democrats?
choices: It suggested that settlers could keep out slavery by refusing to protect it
It said that Congress should ban slavery in all of the territories
It declared that he would leave the Democratic Party to join the Republicans
It called for the repeal of the Fugitive Slave Act in the free states
questions.explanation: Southerners wanted slavery protected in the territories, and Douglas's answer allowed settlers to defeat it in practice.
choiceExplanations: Southerners wanted slavery protected in the territories, and Douglas's answer allowed settlers to defeat it in practice.
Douglas did not call for a congressional ban.
He remained a Democrat.
He did not make that call.
questions.distinguisher: The Congress ban choice is close because Douglas's answer limited slavery, but he relied on settlers and not Congress.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Lincoln's description of slavery as “an apple of discord and an element of division” best supports which claim?
choices: Slavery had been a steady source of conflict between the sections
Slavery had been a bond of union among the states
Slavery had caused the American colonies to separate from Britain
Slavery's critics had caused the conflict by attacking it
questions.explanation: Lincoln says that slavery has “always failed to be a bond of union” and has been “an element of division in the house.”
choiceExplanations: Lincoln says that slavery has “always failed to be a bond of union” and has been “an element of division in the house.”
Lincoln says it had “always failed to be a bond of union.”
The excerpt does not connect slavery to the Revolution.
Lincoln blames slavery and not its critics.
questions.distinguisher: The bond of union choice is close because Lincoln uses those words, but he says slavery had failed to be one.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 5.6, KC-5.2.II.B.ii: the Kansas–Nebraska Act and the Dred Scott decision failed to reduce conflict over slavery in the territories
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Abraham Lincoln, the Republican candidate for the U.S. Senate in Illinois, replying to Stephen A. Douglas in their first debate at Ottawa, Illinois, on August 21, 1858
stimulusBlocks.citation: Abraham Lincoln, reply in the first Lincoln–Douglas debate (Ottawa, Illinois, August 21, 1858), in Noted Speeches of Abraham Lincoln, Including the Lincoln-Douglas Debate. Project Gutenberg eBook #48364.
stimulusBlocks.note: Lincoln is defending his earlier statement, in his “House Divided” speech, that “a house divided against itself cannot stand.” “He” is Douglas, the Democratic senator who wrote the Kansas–Nebraska Act and supported popular sovereignty.
stimulusBlocks.text:
I leave it to you to say whether, in the history of our government, this institution of slavery has not always failed to be a bond of union, and on the contrary been an apple of discord and an element of division in the house. . . .

lately, I think that he, and those acting with him, have placed that institution on a new basis, which looks to the perpetuity and nationalization of slavery. And while it is placed upon this new basis, I say and I have said that I believe we shall not have peace upon the question until the opponents of slavery arrest the further spread of it, and place it where the public mind shall rest in the belief that it is in the course of ultimate extinction; or, on the other hand, that its advocates will push it forward until it shall become alike lawful in all the States, old as well as new, North as well as South.

questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a claim and/or argument in a text-based or non-text-based source.

questions.prompt: Which of the following about Lincoln's situation in August 1858 best explains his argument in the excerpt?
choices: He was the Democratic nominee who wished to win the votes of antislavery Northerners
He was a congressman who had just introduced a bill to ban slavery in the territories
He was the governor of Illinois, preparing the state for a war against the South
He was a Republican candidate trying to persuade voters that Douglas favored the spread of slavery
questions.explanation: Lincoln was running against Douglas for the Senate, and he accused Douglas and his allies of putting slavery “on a new basis.”
choiceExplanations: Douglas, not Lincoln, was the Democrat.
He was not then in Congress.
He held no such office.
Lincoln was running against Douglas for the Senate, and he accused Douglas and his allies of putting slavery “on a new basis.”
questions.distinguisher: The Democratic nominee choice is close because the two men were rivals in the same race, but Douglas was the Democrat and Lincoln the Republican.

questions.prompt: According to Lincoln in the excerpt, what would follow if the spread of slavery were stopped?
choices: Slavery would become lawful in all of the states, old and new, North and South
Slavery would be seen as in the course of ultimate extinction
Slavery would end at once in the states where it already existed
The Supreme Court would overturn the Dred Scott decision on slavery
questions.explanation: Lincoln says that if the opponents of slavery “arrest the further spread of it,” the public mind will “rest in the belief that it is in the course of ultimate extinction.”
choiceExplanations: Lincoln says that would follow if its advocates pushed it forward.
Lincoln says that if the opponents of slavery “arrest the further spread of it,” the public mind will “rest in the belief that it is in the course of ultimate extinction.”
The excerpt speaks of stopping the spread of slavery and not of ending it at once.
The excerpt does not mention the Court.
questions.distinguisher: The lawful in all states choice is close because Lincoln names it, but he says it would follow if slavery's advocates succeeded in pushing it forward.
